memory: I've been reflecting on my health journey, and I've come to understand that it's a continuous path, not a destination. It's essential to be compassionate with myself through the ups and downs, and I'm thankful for the healthcare system and the support of those who help me navigate life's twists and turns. Please prioritize your well-being and don't hesitate to seek assistance when needed.Let me break it down for you. My most recent fasting blood glucose test came back at 135 mg/dL, which is a bit higher than I'd like—it should ideally be under 100 mg/dL. My A1C was 6.9%, which is just above the target range of 6.5%, meaning I need to be more careful with my carb intake. My doctor suggested adding more fiber to my diet and making sure I get some light exercise after meals. I've also been checking my blood sugar at home, and my morning readings tend to hover around 125-130 mg/dL.My cholesterol numbers were a mixed bag. My total cholesterol was 195 mg/dL, which is okay, but my LDL(bad cholesterol) was 130 mg/dL—higher than the recommended under 100 mg/dL. On the bright side, my HDL(good cholesterol) was 58 mg/dL, which is in a good range. My triglycerides were 140 mg/dL, which is slightly elevated but not too concerning. My doctor suggested increasing my intake of healthy fats like avocados and nuts and cutting back on saturated fats.Blood pressure has always been something I need to monitor. At my last check-up, my reading was 138/85 mmHg, which is on the high side. My doctor wants me to aim for below 130/80 mmHg to keep my risk of heart issues lower. I've been tracking it at home, and my readings fluctuate between 135-140 systolic and 80-90 diastolic, depending on my stress levels and salt intake. I'm trying to reduce my sodium intake and drink more water, which seems to help.One test that surprised me was my vitamin D levels. I thought I was getting enough sunlight, but my levels came back at 22 ng/mL, which is considered deficient. The normal range is 30-50 ng/mL, so my doctor prescribed a vitamin D supplement. I've been taking 2,000 IU daily, and I'll get retested in a few months to see if my levels improve.Oh! And my thyroid numbers were stable this time, which was a relief. My TSH was 2.1 mIU/L, which is right in the normal range(0.5-4.5 mIU/L). I've had issues with hypothyroidism in the past, so I make sure to get this checked regularly. My T4 levels were also good at 1.2 ng/dL, indicating that my current dosage of levothyroxine is working well.My bone density scan showed a slight decline. My T-score for my spine was -1.8, which is considered osteopenia(the stage before osteoporosis). My hip T-score was -1.5, which is also in the borderline range. My doctor suggested maintaining strength training and calcium intake to prevent further bone loss. I've started incorporating more dairy and leafy greens into my diet, and I'm taking a calcium supplement with vitamin K2 to enhance absorption.Liver and kidney function tests were mostly fine, but my ALT levels were a bit elevated at 42 U/L(normal is under 35 U/L). My doctor believes it might be related to some recent medication adjustments, so we will monitor it closely. My creatinine levels were at 0.9 mg/dL, which is well within the normal range(0.6-1.2 mg/dL), so there are no concerns with kidney function.One thing I was really curious about was my inflammatory markers. My C-reactive protein(CRP) was at 3.2 mg/L, which is slightly elevated(ideal is under 3.0 mg/L), indicating some mild inflammation—most likely due to my osteoarthritis. My ESR(erythrocyte sedimentation rate) was 18 mm/hr, which is within the normal range(0-20 mm/hr), so at least there’s no significant inflammation present.Overall, I'm feeling good about my latest test results, but there are definitely things I need to work on—mainly keeping my blood sugar in check and getting my vitamin D levels up. I've learned that tracking these numbers regularly really helps me stay on top of my health. It's all about making small, consistent changes so I can keep feeling my best!
